facts.text: In 1817 the German baron Karl von Drais built a two-wheeled machine with no pedals; riders moved it by pushing against the ground with their feet.
The machine was called the Laufmaschine (running machine) and was patented in 1818.
Drais was looking for a way to travel that did not depend on horses.
The running machine had no brakes; riders stopped it with their feet.
The running machine was expensive and riders clashed with people walking on sidewalks; by 1820 the fad was over.
The high-wheeler (penny-farthing) was developed by James Starley and was popular in the 1870s; many found it scary and dangerous to ride.
In 1885 John Kemp Starley, James Starley's nephew, began testing in Coventry a chain-driven bicycle with two much smaller wheels, which became the Rover safety bicycle.
In February 1888 John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish veterinarian in Belfast, made air-filled rubber-and-canvas tubes for the wheels of his young son's tricycle.
When the safety bicycle was paired with air-filled tires, the ride became softer and about 30 percent faster.
In the 1890s many women took up cycling and gave up heavy Victorian skirts for lighter clothes.
Cyclists pushed for better roads, and in 1895 Brooklyn opened one of the first bike paths in the United States.
The UN marks World Bicycle Day on 3 June and calls the bicycle a simple, affordable and clean means of transport.
The UN says cycling helps cut air pollution and traffic and lowers the risk of illnesses such as heart disease.
